nameStory: The Common Driftclinger gets its name from its habit of clinging to driftwood and debris that washes up along shorelines. These little crustaceans are masters at hanging onto floating wood as it travels across oceans, which helps explain how they've spread to coastlines around the world.
description: The Common Driftclinger is a small, oval-shaped woodlouse (also called a pillbug or roly-poly) that lives along ocean shores. Unlike their garden-dwelling cousins, these marine isopods are specially adapted for life in the splash zone where waves meet land. They're typically about half an inch long with a segmented, armored body that can roll into a tight ball when threatened. Despite being called a woodlouse, they're actually crustaceans - more closely related to shrimp and crabs than insects.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Distinctly oval and flattened, with a smooth, shiny shell that feels hard like a tiny crab's back when gently touched

idTips.label: Coastal habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively in the splash zone of rocky shores, under driftwood, and in crevices where salt spray reaches but never far from the ocean

idTips.label: Rolling behavior
idTips.description: Rolls into a perfect ball when disturbed, making a tiny clicking sound as the segments lock together

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Mottled gray-brown with lighter patches, often taking on the weathered color of the driftwood they live under

idTips.label: Movement style
idTips.description: Scuttles quickly with a distinctive side-to-side motion, much faster than terrestrial pillbugs

habitat: Look for Common Driftclingers in the splash zone of rocky New England coastlines, especially around Casco Bay in Maine and the rocky shores of New Hampshire and Massachusetts. They hide under driftwood, seaweed, and in rock crevices where they stay moist from salt spray but avoid being submerged by waves. You'll often find them alongside periwinkles and barnacles in this harsh intertidal environment.

seasonality.spring: Most active as warming temperatures bring them out from winter hiding spots. Look under freshly deposited storm debris and driftwood.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to spot scurrying around coastal debris during low tide. Often found in small groups under the same piece of wood.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek deeper shelter. Storm seasons may wash them into new areas along with fresh driftwood.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in rock crevices and under heavy debris. Rarely seen unless you carefully move their shelter on warmer days.

funFact: These tiny ocean hitchhikers are living proof that the sea connects all continents - the exact same species that you find clinging to driftwood in Maine also lives on beaches in Australia, South Africa, and remote Pacific islands, having traveled the world's oceans as stowaways on floating debris for millions of years.
confusionNotes: Easily confused with common garden pillbugs, but remember the location rule: if it's near the ocean's splash zone, it's likely a Driftclinger; if it's in your garden or forest, it's a terrestrial woodlouse. Driftclingers also move much more quickly and have a shinier, more streamlined appearance.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'woodlice' or 'pillbugs,' these are actually marine crustaceans that breathe through gills, not insects or true bugs. This creates confusion since they look similar to terrestrial isopods but represent an ancient lineage that never fully left the sea.
compareHints: As the only Armadilloniscus species commonly found in New England, compare it with other coastal isopods in the Detonidae family by noting its distinctly oval shape and perfect ball-rolling ability. Other marine isopods in the region tend to be more elongated and can't roll up as completely, plus they're usually found deeper in the intertidal zone rather than the high splash zone.
